I'm pretty much on board with @fchollet here. I'd add a little more nuance, since we can't be 💯 certain. But he gives the right intuitions for why current AI is vanishingly unlikely to be conscious, and he's absolutely right about the dystopian outcomes that would follow from treating it as if it is.

I make the broader case against conscious AI in this @NoemaMag essay https://t.co/LmSiQnTHLP, and in long form in this @BBSJournal collection https://t.co/6ZFzHrV0Kp (with arguments from all sides in the commentaries) 👇🏽

reviewedPosts.author: anilkseth
reviewedPosts.text:
Fair enough 🙏🏽. I should have said I was making my own point (perhaps in line with Matt). This point remains that I cannot see any upsides to creating avatars that are indistinguishable from real humans, and major downsides, over and above the (already dubious) merits of creating AI systems that are anthropomimetic.  

In other words, I think (i) it would be sensible to minimise the anthropomimesis of AI wherever possible while still sufficient for the task, and (ii) there is no legitimate case that I can see that warrants going all the way to full indistinguishability. Creating avatars that cannot be distinguished from human beings should not be allowed.

(Agreed, anthropo-equivalence is not a great term.  I was searching for something that connoted full indistinguishability rather than mere similarity.)

reviewedPosts.author: anilkseth
reviewedPosts.text:
Hi @dioscuri, with respect, I think you're missing the point. The brouhaha about Griffin is not about building anthropomimetic AI. This has upsides and downsides (more of the latter IMO). It is specifically about creating avatars that are *empirically indistinguishable* from human beings, with video and audio now allowed.  

I do not see any legitimate motivation whatsoever for what we might call "anthropo-equivalent AI", beyond mere anthropomimesis.  Instead, I see massive potential for disaster.

As I'm sure you know, Daniel Dennett gave some of these reasons back in 2023: https://t.co/Hl3NhUdFzz

reviewedPosts.author: fchollet
reviewedPosts.text:
Side note. The idea that current models are conscious is absurd and downright offensive. Do not confuse competent information processing and sentience, they are wholly unrelated.

You can be entirely incompetent at everything yet fully conscious, like a toddler, or extraordinarily competent in one or more domains with absolutely zero consciousness, like a calculator, a chess engine, a self-driving car, or an AI chatbot.

Possessing the "circuits" for competent information processing in a given domain, whether through training or hardcoding, does not produce qualia, subjective experience, emotions, or suffering. Calculators do not "feel" arithmetic and they don't get tired or annoyed when you give them larger numbers to process. To argue otherwise is ontologically absurd. Current AI models are effectively calculators scaled to a very large number of competence circuits across many domains, etched via gradient descent.

reviewedPosts.author: fchollet
reviewedPosts.text:
The notion that current AI models are sentient and can suffer, combined with the foolish idea that suffering can be mathematically quantified and weighted between humans and non-humans, could lead us down an incredibly dark and dystopian path.

But before it gets to that point, it will rightfully be met with immense backlash from team humans.
